title: MEART: The semi-living artist
extended_summary:
This paper describes MEART (Multi-Electrode Array aRT), a neurorobotic art project that linked a living culture of rat cortical neurons to a robotic drawing machine. The authors frame the work as an exploration of embodied intelligence, creativity, learning, and the relationship between art and science, rather than as a conventional educational intervention or classroom study.

The intervention consisted of a closed-loop system in which neural activity from cultured rat neurons recorded on a multi-electrode array was translated into motor commands for a drawing robot, while camera-based images of the evolving drawing were transformed into electrical feedback stimuli for the neurons. The paper also describes a simulated animat version used to refine the training algorithm and compare goal-directed adaptation under a virtual body.

The context was gallery exhibitions and laboratory experimentation, with the biological network maintained in Atlanta while the robotic body operated in exhibitions across multiple international locations. The paper reports that fixed training stimuli could induce neural plasticity without reliable goal-directed behavioral success in the real robot, whereas the adaptive training algorithm worked better in the simulated animat. The authors conclude that the project demonstrates a platform for studying embodiment, plasticity, and public engagement with neuroscience, but it is not evidence of K-12 science learning or AI-assisted instruction.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/art-science and methods paper about a neurorobotic installation, not a K-12 education study. It does not evaluate an educational AI intervention, and there is no causal comparison on student science outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: No K-12 science learning or inquiry impact is reported. The paper’s findings concern robotics/neural plasticity and artistic exhibition, so there is no measurable educational effect to classify.
